phrases.english_text: Yeah, they had gardens. My dad was a planter. He planted corn and strawberries. The workers plowed for the plants to grow. We were all sitting there, us older ones. Like, Juanita. They left their kids for us to babysit. “Look!” she said. The cows came, a whole lot of them. They belonged to the Starrs. The cows roamed in the woods back then. She said, “Look! Let’s open it! The cows are bringing calves, let’s get milk from them.” We believed them, so we opened it. Those cows just came running in, fast, when we opened it. They were wanting the corn! [laughter] She said, “Ooh! They’re ruining the corn!” Then we had to chase them off. Then when Dad got home, we almost got killed. He turned around and picked up the hoes. “Let’s plow up the cow tracks!” So, we plowed just where the cows’ tracks were hiding. And the corn was standing up.

phrases.english_text: Really. Me and my sister, we spoke it growing up. When I started school, the teachers weren’t letting me speak Cherokee. They were hitting me like this [gestures]. phrases.english_text: She was the one that was telling about it. They talked about what she used to talk about. They just mostly talked about boogers. phrases.english_text: That Ned Longbird she’s talking about, he was always walking on the road. He was always picking up anything on the road, no matter how hot it was! And he’d have on a big coat. He’ll have things in a bag. We lived nearby and when he came and we’d be sitting, my late father would say hello. Ned would come up to the porch and go inside the house. If there was something there, like bread, he would take it all and come back out and go on. [laughter] “Yeah, come back again!” Dad would tell him. That’s how Ned Longbird was. He was a good person and he was old, but he was walking good on the road. He would pick anything up on the road and put it in his pocket ’cause he had on a big coat all the time.

phrases.english_text: It would be all night! Nowadays, it has to be far away before you can spend the night. Back then, if they lived in walking distance, you would spend the night. There was an old man named Diganotsatl(i) who lived there. We lived way up on the hill from him. We would go there with our mom. We would spend the night. When they said, “You all spend the night here!” we would spend the night. There was a man named Tsusolvd(i). He was Diganotsatl(i)’s son. He said, “Lillie! Let’s just lie here! If the rooster crows, it’ll be sitting right above us! I just hope it don’t poop on you!” he said. “Haw!” I told him. I was laying real close to him, him with his overalls on. He didn’t even take his overalls off. Me and Tsusolvd(i) were in bed. And then in the morning, the rooster crowed. There was a board across there, because there was no wall, just sheetrock. That’s where the rooster was standing, right above where I was laying. I got up. I thought it was going to poop on me! They thought it was funny, and they laughed at me.

phrases.english_text: That’s how we were something. We lived closer this way. I remember, sometimes we were all scattered laying, sleeping outside on the porch in the summer. This [gestures] way lived the late Nellie Mays. She lived there with her husband, Gill Mayes. That’s who would wake us up on the porch in the mornings.
